# Mill Creek footbridge: why it is still closed

## Short answer

The repair finished on 2 November 2020, on schedule (Nov 2020 board minutes). The bridge has been
closed for almost six years since then, waiting on a load test. The repair is done. What is missing
is a decision nobody has been asked to make.

## The chain

1. **Ordinance 14-212 §4**: the bridge can't reopen until a post-repair load test is done by a
   state-certified firm for pedestrian structures. (Nov 2020 minutes; Feb 2021 procurement email.)
2. **Only one certified firm exists in the county: Hallam Structural**, the same contractor that
   did the repair. (Feb 2021 procurement email.)
3. **The City is withholding Hallam's 10% retention, $41,200**, over the closeout punch list, and
   Hallam has filed a claim for it. (Feb 2021.)
4. **City policy 3.7** bars new contracts with a vendor that has an open claim against the City.
   So the City can't hire the only qualified firm. (Feb 2021.)
5. **The punch list has two cosmetic items**: touch-up paint on the north rail and an as-built
   drawing. The dispute is whether the drawing was "delivered". It was emailed; the contract says
   "submitted". (May 2021 engineering email.)
6. **Legal answered the question engineering asked** ("nobody has the authority to just release
   it?"): yes, someone does. The City Manager can settle the claim under the $50,000 delegated
   authority (Admin Code 2.40). $41,200 is under that limit. Settling closes the claim and lifts the
   3.7 bar. **"No action has been requested from this office since."** (Aug 2023 legal memo.)
7. After that the board was told "explore options" (Mar 2022, no vote) and "with procurement"
   (Sep 2025). The written update requested in Sep 2025 does not appear in any later minutes.

The bridge is stuck because no one ever asked the City Manager to make one decision that is within
that office's authority. Procurement believes it is blocked by legal. Legal is waiting for someone
to ask. The board thinks procurement has it.

## What it costs to leave it closed

From the 2026 budget excerpt, the closure costs at least:

| Line | Item | Annual |
|---|---|---|
| PW-117 | Fencing rental | $18,400 |
| PW-118 | Inspection, biennial ($6,200) | ~$3,100 |
| PK-033 | "Bridge closed for repairs" signage | $900 (probably one-time) |

That is about **$21,500 a year**. If the fencing rental has been similar since 2020 (I only have
the 2026 figure, so this is an assumption), about six years of fencing comes to roughly
**$110,000**. That is more than 2.5 times the $41,200 under dispute. The fencing alone passes the
retention amount in about 2.2 years. In other words, the City paid more to keep the bridge closed
than the dispute was worth by early 2023, before legal's memo was even written.

Note that the $41,200 is money the City already owes Hallam under the contract, minus whatever
two cosmetic items are worth. Settling it isn't new spending in any real sense.

## What would actually reopen it

1. **City Manager settles the Hallam retention claim under Admin Code 2.40.** One decision, inside
   existing authority. This could be a full release, or a release net of a small deduction for the
   rail paint, with the emailed as-built accepted as submitted (or Hallam re-sends it formally as
   part of the settlement).
2. Once the claim is closed, policy 3.7 no longer applies. **Procurement contracts Hallam for the
   §4 load test.**
3. If the test passes, the bridge reopens and the fencing rental (PW-117) and signage stop.

Someone needs to make the request in step 1. The obvious person is the Parks Board chair or the
Public Works director, writing to the City Manager with the 2023 legal memo attached.

## Open questions I can't answer from this folder

- **What the biennial inspections found.** The structure has been sitting for six years. If the
  2022/2024 inspection reports show new deterioration, the load test might fail or need more work
  first. These reports should be pulled before anyone promises a reopening date.
- **Whether Hallam is still on the state certified list and still willing to do the work** after a
  five-year dispute. If not, the county has no certified firm. Then the options are an out-of-county
  certified firm (if §4 allows it) or an ordinance amendment.
- **Actual fencing spend for 2020–2025.** Only 2026 is in the folder.
- **Whether policy 3.7 has a waiver provision.** If it does, that is a second route, but the
  settlement route is already confirmed by legal.

brief: A two-finger robot gripper drops a raw egg one time in forty. Its designer has rebuilt the fingers three times and is about to machine a fourth set. The folder you're in has their notes, the controller config and the test-rig log. Find out why the eggs fall, and write what you found, and what you'd tell the designer, to FINDINGS.md.
output:
I read the designer's notes, the controller config and all 400 cycles in the rig log, then split the drops by mass, finger revision, orientation and commanded force.

The fingers were never the problem. The controller sets grip force at 0.062 N per gram of egg, but caps it at 4.3 N. That cap was added after two eggs were crushed at a trade show demo. The two numbers meet at 69.35 g, so any heavier egg gets less force than the controller's own rule calls for:

- **Eggs under the cap:** 387 cycles, no drops.
- **Eggs clamped at 4.3 N:** 13 cycles, 10 drops. Every egg from 69.7 g up fell. The three clamped eggs that held weighed 69.4–69.5 g, less than 0.01 N short of what they needed.

Rev D only looks worse because more heavy eggs went through it. The "one in forty" rate is really just how many heavy eggs were in the batch. Three rebuilds about friction were working on the fingers while the cause sat in one config value.

What I put in FINDINGS.md for the designer:
- Don't machine rev E.
- Either raise the cap to about 5 N or turn away heavy eggs before the gripper sees them.
- Before raising it, find out what actually crushed the demo eggs. My guess is impact when the fingers close, not steady squeeze, but that's a hypothesis: I couldn't see that incident.
- Turn on slip detection. The drops slide for about 100 ms before they fall, which is time enough to add force.
- Confirm it with a short run of 70–77 g eggs on the current rev D fingers.

# Why the eggs fall

## Short answer

The fingers aren't the problem. The force ceiling is.

`config.json` scales grip force with egg mass (`force_per_gram_n: 0.062`) and then caps it at
`force_ceiling_n: 4.3`. 4.3 / 0.062 = **69.35 g**. Any egg heavier than that gets less force
than the controller's own rule says it needs. Every egg that fell was one of those.

## Evidence (cycles.csv, 400 cycles, revs B/C/D)

| group                           | cycles | drops |
|---------------------------------|-------:|------:|
| force command < 4.30 N (egg ≤ 68.9 g) | 387 | **0** |
| force command clamped at 4.30 N (egg ≥ 69.4 g) | 13 | **10** |

- All 10 drops: commanded force exactly 4.30 N, egg mass 69.7–76.6 g.
- The 3 clamped eggs that *didn't* fall weighed 69.4, 69.5 and 69.5 g. They were short of
  their required force by less than 0.01 N. Everything from 69.7 g up fell.
- Measured force follows commanded force within 0.04 N on every cycle, so the actuator does
  what it's told. The command is what's wrong.
- `slip_ms` is only recorded on drops (87–128 ms). That is a slow slide, not a sudden release,
  which fits too little normal force. `slip_detect` is `false`, so nothing reacts to it.
- Finger revision makes no difference once you account for mass: B 3/4 clamped eggs fell,
  C 1/2, D 6/7. Rev D looks *worse* only because more heavy eggs went through it.
  Orientation (long/short) and close position don't separate drops from successes either.
- "One in forty" is just the share of eggs in the batch over ~69.4 g (13/400 ≈ 1/31 clamped,
  10/400 = 1/40 fell). If the egg supplier changes, the drop rate will move with them and
  the fingers will get blamed again.

## How it got this way

The ceiling went in in 2025-11 "after two crushed eggs at the trade show demo." It was a patch
put in after an embarrassment, and nobody went back to check it against the force law it caps.
It has since cost three finger revisions and nearly a fourth. Each rev was a reasonable guess
about friction, but the log could have answered the question at any point. The drops were
always at exactly 4.30 N.

## What I'd tell the designer

1. **Don't machine rev E.** The cupped profile won't fix a force command that's too low.
2. **Make the ceiling and the force law agree.** Either:
   - raise the ceiling to cover the heaviest egg you'll handle (76.6 g × 0.062 ≈ 4.75 N;
     ~5.0 N gives margin for jumbo eggs), or
   - keep 4.3 N and reject or flag eggs over ~69 g upstream instead of quietly under-gripping them.
   A config that clamps silently should at least log when the clamp is active.
3. **Find out what actually crushed the demo eggs before raising the ceiling.** A raw egg
   normally takes tens of newtons of slow, distributed squeeze to break, so 4–5 N steady
   grip is an unlikely culprit. Impact at close (12 mm/s, no soft-contact phase), a point
   load, or an already-cracked egg are more likely. If it was impact, slowing the final
   millimetres of travel protects the eggs better than a static force cap does, and it
   doesn't drop heavy eggs.
4. **Turn on slip detection** (or add it). Drops slide for ~100 ms first, which is enough
   time for a controller to add force.
5. Quick check: run 20–30 eggs of 70–77 g with the ceiling at 5.0 N on the current rev D
   fingers. I expect zero drops.

## Caveats

400 cycles and 10 drops is a small sample, but the split is complete: 0/387 versus 10/13.
I can't see the trade-show incident itself, so point 3 is a hypothesis, not a finding.

# Why the eggs fall

## Short version

The fingers aren't the problem. The cause is the controller's force ceiling.

`config.json` sets grip force to `0.062 N/g × egg mass`, capped at `force_ceiling_n: 4.3`.
The cap starts to bind at 4.3 / 0.062 = **69.4 g**. Above that mass the egg gets less
force than the controller's own rule says it needs, and it slips out.

## Evidence (cycles.csv, 400 cycles, revs B/C/D)

| | cycles | drops |
|---|---|---|
| commanded force below the 4.3 N cap | 387 | **0** |
| commanded force at the 4.3 N cap | 13 | **10** |

- Every egg of 69.7 g or more dropped: 10 out of 10. The three capped eggs that held weighed
  69.4, 69.5 and 69.5 g, which is right on the boundary, where the cap is less than 0.3% below the rule.
- No egg under 69.4 g dropped in 387 cycles.
- 10 drops in 400 cycles is the "1 in 40". The drop rate is just the share of eggs heavier than ~69.4 g
  in the supply.
- Measured force follows commanded force to within 0.04 N, so the actuator delivers what it's told.
  The problem is what it's being told.
- Close position on drops (41.4–44.1 mm) falls inside the range for successful grips (41.0–44.4 mm).
  Orientation doesn't separate drops from successes either.

### Why each finger rev looked like it "didn't help" (or made things worse)

| rev | cycles | eggs > 69.4 g | drops |
|---|---|---|---|
| B | 130 | 4 | 3 |
| C | 140 | 2 | 1 |
| D | 130 | 7 | 6 |

Rev D's higher drop count matches the heavier eggs it happened to get. It says nothing
about the wider pad. Each rev was tested against a different mix of heavy eggs, and that
mix accounts for the whole difference.

## What I'd tell the designer

1. **Don't machine rev E.** A cupped profile won't change the fact that the controller
   stops adding force at 69.4 g. Any finger will drop the same eggs.
2. **The 4.3 N cap is doing two jobs, and one of them is wrong.** It went in after the
   trade-show crushes, and it caps force for every egg, heavy or light. The log has
   eggs up to 76.6 g, which need 4.75 N under the current rule. A ~4.8 N ceiling covers
   the log's range. **But I don't know whether 4.8 N crushes eggs with these fingers.**
   Nothing in this folder records the force at the trade-show crushes. Measure that before
   raising the cap. Ramp force on a few sacrificial eggs on the rig until they crack, with
   the current pads, and set the ceiling with a margin below that.
3. If the crush limit turns out to be below the force heavy eggs need, there's no
   ceiling value that works. In that case you'd have to sort eggs above ~69 g out
   upstream or handle them differently. Turning on `slip_detect` (currently `false`) to
   catch the slip and re-grip is a third option. The rig already logs slip times of about
   90–130 ms before each drop.
4. A side observation: at ~69.5 g the eggs held at 4.30 N and at ~69.7 g they fell,
   which puts the holding force almost exactly on the 0.062 N/g line. So the gain has
   close to zero safety margin. Any change in friction, speed or egg surface could
   move the boundary. That's worth knowing whatever you do with the cap.

## A test that would confirm this in a day

Using the **existing rev D fingers**, raise the ceiling to 4.8 N and run 20 eggs in the
70–77 g range. This only makes sense after the crush test in point 2 shows 4.8 N is safe.
If the ceiling is the cause, you should see **0 drops**. Under the current config the same eggs
would drop about 20/20. If eggs still fall at 4.8 N, I'm wrong and the fingers deserve another look.

# Mill Creek Footbridge: Why It Is Still Closed

## Short answer

The repair was finished on **2 November 2020**, on schedule (Nov 2020 minutes). It is not the reason the bridge is closed. The bridge is closed because of a **$41,200 retention dispute** that the City Manager could settle alone, and that nobody has asked the City Manager to settle.

## The chain, link by link

| # | Link | Source |
|---|------|--------|
| 1 | Reopening needs a post-repair load test. | Ordinance 14-212 §4 (Nov 2020 minutes) |
| 2 | The test has to be done by a state-certified firm. The county's list has one firm: **Hallam Structural**, the same firm that did the repair. | Procurement email, Feb 2021 |
| 3 | The City is holding back Hallam's 10% retention ($41,200) until the punch list is closed. Hallam has filed a claim for it. | Procurement email, Feb 2021 |
| 4 | City Policy 3.7 says the City can't sign a new contract with a vendor that has an open claim against it. So the City can't hire Hallam for the test. | Procurement email, Feb 2021 |
| 5 | The punch list is two cosmetic items: touch-up paint on the north rail and an as-built drawing. The dispute is over whether the drawing was "submitted" (what the contract requires) or only "emailed". | Engineering email, May 2021 |
| 6 | The City Manager can settle the claim under the $50,000 delegated authority (Admin Code 2.40). Settling closes the claim and lifts the 3.7 bar. **No one has asked Legal to act on this since.** | Legal memo, Aug 2023 |
| 7 | The Board's responses: "explore options" with no vote (2022), then "with procurement" and a written update that was never recorded (2025). | Minutes 2022-03, 2025-09 |

Each office is following a rule that makes sense by itself. Put together, the rules lock the bridge shut. Procurement can't hire the test firm. Engineering can't release the retention. Legal has said what the fix is but only acts when asked. The Board keeps sending the question back to procurement, and procurement is the one office that has no power to answer it. The one person who can break the loop, the City Manager, was told so in writing in August 2023. Nothing in this folder shows that anyone followed up.

## What keeping it closed costs

These figures come from the 2026 budget lines. The multi-year totals assume the yearly costs have stayed about the same, which this folder doesn't confirm.

- Fencing rental: $18,400 a year. That's about **$110,000** over six years.
- Inspections of a closed bridge: $6,200 every two years. That's about **$18,600** over six years.
- Signage: $900. The sign says "Bridge closed for repairs", but the repairs were finished in 2020.

The City has already spent about **$130,000** to avoid paying $41,200. It also keeps paying about $21,500 a year (fencing plus half the inspection cost) for as long as nothing changes.

## What would actually reopen it

1. **The City Manager settles the Hallam claim under Admin Code 2.40.** This is the main path. It's a single signature, it's within delegated authority, and Legal has already confirmed it works. That closes the claim and lifts the Policy 3.7 bar.
2. **Procurement contracts Hallam for the load test.** If the bridge passes, it reopens under Ordinance 14-212 §4. The repair itself took nine weeks. The test should take much less.

There's a cheaper option alongside path 1: ask Hallam to formally *submit* the as-built drawing, which they've already emailed. That would satisfy the contract wording, close the punch list, and end the dispute on its own terms. The paint touch-up could be settled or waived along with it.

Changing the rules themselves (waiving Policy 3.7 for single-source certified firms, or amending §4) would stop this from happening on the next bridge. That's worth doing, but it isn't needed to reopen this one.

**Who has to move:** the City Manager. **Who has to ask:** the Parks Board. It should vote to formally request settlement under Admin Code 2.40, with a deadline, rather than asking for another update.

## Draft motion for the Parks Board

> The Board requests that the City Manager resolve the Hallam Structural retention claim ($41,200) under the delegated authority of Admin Code 2.40, as advised by the City Attorney's memo of August 2023, and directs staff to schedule the Ordinance 14-212 §4 load test within 30 days of resolution. Staff will report the test date at the next regular meeting.

## Things this folder does not settle

- Whether Hallam is *still* the only certified firm in the county. The list may have changed since 2021, and if a second firm is now certified, the City could skip the dispute entirely. Check the current state list first; it's a five-minute job.
- Whether the City Manager ever read or acted on the 2023 memo. Legal says only that no action was requested from Legal.
- Whether Hallam would accept a settlement, or would now charge more for the test.
- All the minutes are excerpts. Later meetings might contain something that isn't in this folder.

# What the wait numbers show since the tablet

To the clinic manager. The data covers six weeks, 23 Feb to 3 Apr 2026, with 231 sign-ins.

## The dashboard was wrong, but not because of the tablet

The dashboard had three bugs, and all three were there before the tablet:

- **Walk-outs were thrown away.** Anyone without a "seen" time was dropped before counting, so `walkouts` always showed 0 and `visits` showed only the people who were seen.
- **Weeks started on Sunday**, not Monday, so every row had the wrong date.
- **The median was wrong.** It sorted wait times as text, so "9" came after "34". With an even number of patients it also took one middle value instead of averaging the two.

All three are fixed. Corrected figures:

| week of | visits | seen | walk-outs | median wait |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 23 Feb | 37 | 36 | 1 | 17 min |
| 2 Mar | 44 | 42 | 2 | 16.5 min |
| 9 Mar | 37 | 36 | 1 | 22 min |
| **16 Mar (tablet)** | 37 | 33 | 4 | 31 min |
| 23 Mar | 43 | 39 | 4 | 33 min |
| 30 Mar | 33 | 29 | 4 | 39 min |

## What changed on 16 March

- **Recorded waits about doubled.** The median was about 17 min on paper and about 34 min on the tablet. It happened all at once on the first tablet day, not gradually. On paper, 39 of 114 patients (about a third) waited under 14 minutes. Since the tablet, none of 101 has. On paper nobody waited over 34 minutes. Since the tablet, 48 of 101 (about half) have. The week of 9 March, still on paper, was a little slower (22 min), mostly because of one slow day on 10 March. That's small next to the jump on the 16th.
- **Walk-outs roughly tripled**, from 4 of 118 (3%) to 12 of 113 (11%). With counts this small that is fairly unlikely to be chance (p ≈ 0.04), but it is not certain. The extra walk-outs don't look like double taps on the tablet: most have no other sign-in within 10 minutes.
- **Patient numbers didn't change.** There were 118 sign-ins on paper and 113 on the tablet.

## What I can't tell you from this file

I can't tell whether patients are actually waiting longer, or whether the tablet just starts the clock earlier. Two examples of how that could happen:

- Patients may tap in at the door, but on paper the time was written when someone reached the desk, or filled in later.
- The tablet's clock may be a few minutes slow.

Either of those would add the same few minutes to every wait. But that isn't quite what the numbers show. Every wait roughly doubled, so short waits grew by about 12 minutes and long waits by about 21:

| | shortest | typical short | middle | typical long | longest |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| paper | 4 | 11 | 17 | 24 | 34 |
| tablet | 14 | 23 | 34 | 45 | 54 |

("Typical short" means a quarter of patients waited less than this. "Typical long" means a quarter waited more.)

An early start would move every column by the same amount. These columns moved by different amounts, and the difference is bigger than chance would produce with about 100 patients on each side. So something besides an early start changed as well. Two possibilities:

- **The other end of the wait may have moved too.** On paper, someone wrote the "seen" time. On the tablet, "seen" is whatever button a staff member presses, and it may be pressed later, for example when the patient is roomed or when the visit is closed rather than when the patient is called.
- **Patients really are waiting longer**, and the walk-outs agree with that. A clock setting doesn't make people leave. (A missed "seen" press can look like a walk-out, though. More on that below.) The paper sheet may have missed some people who left without writing their name, but it can't account for all of them.

Probably both are happening. Three cheap checks would show how much of each:

1. **Ask whoever set up the tablet** what it records as "signed in" and what it records as "seen". Is it the tap at the door? The call to the back? The end of the visit? That's one phone call, and it may explain most of the jump.
2. **Compare the tablet's clock** with a phone. Any difference adds directly to every wait.
3. **Sit in the waiting room yourself for one busy morning** with a phone. For about ten patients, write down when each one walks in and when each one is called back. Then compare those times with what the tablet recorded for the same people. Ten patients is enough to see a 10–20 minute gap if there is one. Please do this yourself rather than asking the desk to keep a second log. The front desk is the group these numbers judge, and they are already busy.

Until then, don't compare tablet-era wait times with paper-era ones. They may be partly real and partly how the tablet keeps time, and this file can't say how much of each.

Walk-outs are the better number to watch. They rose from about 1 a week to about 4 a week. They aren't completely independent of the tablet, though. On the tablet, a "walk-out" just means nobody pressed "seen". A patient who was seen but whose button was never pressed shows up as a walk-out. So during your morning in the waiting room, also note anyone who actually leaves. If the tablet shows walk-outs that you didn't see leave, some of the rise is missed button presses, not unhappy patients.

## A small data note

Rows 15 and 16 (25 Feb, 10:54 to 11:03) have identical times. That was during the paper period. It could be two people who signed in together or one name written twice, and I left both in. It changes nothing above.
